item.title: Two-Dimensional Materials toward CMOS-Compatible Scalable Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Evaluates feasibility, integration pathways, and performance tradeoffs of incorporating atomically thin 2D materials into CMOS-compatible solid-state quantum processor fabrication.

Grade 0.486 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Mara Lieberegts, Ye Wang

Asks

Can 2D material fabrication techniques developed for advanced CMOS electronics address interface disorder, chemical residue, and scalability limits in solid-state quantum hardware?

But

Perspective/review analysis without new primary experimental datasets.

Tools

2D materials · van der Waals heterostructures · CMOS-compatible nanofabrication · solid-state qubit architectures

Abstract

Manufacturability is one of several constraints on developing solid-state quantum processors, along with qubit performance, control, connectivity, cryogenic operation, and fault tolerance. Chemical residues, structural disorder, and non-uniform interfaces introduced during fabrication can compromise qubit coherence. Two-dimensional (2D) materials, with their atomically thin crystals and van der Waals interfaces, offer routes to address some of these challenges. Their concurrent development as next-generation CMOS channel materials motivates an examination of whether relevant processes can be transferred to quantum chips. This Perspective evaluates the opportunities and limitations of 2D materials for CMOS-compatible quantum hardware.

item.title: Phase-stable voltage bias for Josephson photonics devices
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Coherent phase reference transferred from a Josephson voltage standard via superconducting order parameter increases ICTA averaged gain by 14 dB to ~27 dB and achieves degenerate phase-sensitive amplification.

Grade 0.474 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Amir Hosein Esmaeili, Naveen Nehra, Alexandre Paquette, Mona Arabmohammadi, Baptiste Monge, Alexandre Rogalle, Francois Cyrenne-Bergeron, Yannick Lapointe, Nicolas Lavoie, Nicolas Bourlet, Max Hofheinz

Figure

Gain and noise versus frequency for unstabilized and JVS-stabilized ICTA. Activating the JVS at 12 GHz locks the Josephson frequency over a ±50 MHz bias range, boosts peak gain from 13 dB to 27 dB, and reaches input noise of 0.5 photons at degeneracy.

Asks

How can a stable phase reference be provided to dc-biased Josephson photonics devices to suppress voltage-noise-induced linewidth broadening and enable phase-coherent parametric operation?

Before

Unstabilized ICTA had maximum gain of 13 dB, ~1.5 photon input-referred noise, and lacked degenerate phase-sensitive features due to phase diffusion across >2π within ~30 ns.

But

Millikelvin operation with low RF power (-65 dBm to -40 dBm). Resonator linewidth Γ/2π ≈ 1.2 GHz. Squeezing deforms into an S-shape at 31 dB gain due to amplifier saturation.

Tools

Josephson voltage standard (JVS) · Inelastic Cooper-pair tunneling amplifier (ICTA) · Superconducting on-chip low-pass filter · SQUID

Abstract

Parametric interactions are foundational to superconducting quantum technologies, yet conventional microwave-driven pumping introduces parasitic Kerr nonlinearities and higher-order harmonics that limit device performance. Josephson Photonics (JP) avoids these parasitics by utilizing dc-biased junctions but has remained constrained by high phase noise and the absence of a stable phase reference. Here, we overcome this limitation by integrating a Josephson voltage standard (JVS) to establish a noise-tolerant phase reference, and demonstrate that this reference is coherently transferred to an inelastic Cooper-pair tunneling amplifier (ICTA) via the superconducting order parameter.The resulting low-phase-noise architecture yields a 14-dB enhancement in averaged gain and better quantum-limited noise performance. Critically, the phase reference enables the first observation of phase-sensitive gain and sqeezing in a dc-biased amplifier. By reconciling clean, Kerr-free nonlinearities with phase-coherent drive, our architecture establishes a robust platform for high-purity parametric processes in superconducting circuits.

item.title: Two-qubit gates for the soft 0-π qubit
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft 0-π qubits achieves simulated fidelity of approximately 99.9% at gate time of approximately 160 ns.

Grade 0.467 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity” · Zhenxing Liu, Eli Weissler, Joshua Combes

Figure

Gate error (1−F) versus gate time tg for the CZ gate under closed-system unitary evolution and open-system noise models with coherence times T1=Tϕ=T∈{3,30,170}μs.

Asks

Can an unprotected two-qubit gate with high fidelity and short duration be designed for experimentally realizable soft 0-π superconducting qubits?

But

Simulated in zero-disorder limit with identical circuit components; uses phenomenological noise model with reduced 60-level Hilbert subspace.

Tools

capacitively coupled soft 0-π Hamiltonian · Lindblad master equation · Gaussian drive pulses on n_θ mode · dressed-state truncation

Abstract

The 0-π qubit promises longer lifetimes than the transmon, making it a strong candidate for a next-generation, lower-error qubit. Gyenis et al. experimentally demonstrated an unprotected single-qubit gate in the soft 0-π regime [1], but no corresponding two-qubit gate has yet been proposed. We propose an unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft 0-π qubits. The gate uses a direct transition between a computational state and a higher non-computational state. Assuming negligible device disorder and a phenomenological noise model, the simulated CZ gate achieves a fidelity of approximately 99.9% at a gate time of approximately 160 ns.

item.title: Quantum Simulation of Two-Dimensional Free Dirac Hamiltonian in Multimode Circuit QED
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Implemented a programmable 2+1D free massive Dirac Hamiltonian in multimode circuit QED. Observed rotational Zitterbewegung whose oscillation frequency increases while amplitude decreases with higher effective mass ΔΩ.

Grade 0.436 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Jiwon Kang, Jiuk Lee, Eliya Blumenthal, Shay Hacohen-Gourgy, Eunseong Kim

Figure

Trajectories and time traces of the simulated 2D position quadratures ⟨Xˆ1⟩ and ⟨Xˆ2⟩. Measured data match open-system simulations showing mass-dependent rotational Zitterbewegung loops.

Asks

Can a fully programmable two-dimensional massive Dirac Hamiltonian, with dynamical quantum operators for both momentum components, be simulated in circuit QED?

Before

1D Dirac dynamics and 2D massless Weyl dynamics were demonstrated in trapped ions, while photonic lattices and fixed-coupling superconducting circuits lacked independent dynamical quantum momentum degrees of freedom.

But

Fidelity bounded by transmon charging energy Ec/h=230 MHz limiting drive power, spin-locking decoherence (T2ρ=17 μs), non-RWA terms, and ±5 kHz Rabi calibration uncertainty.

Tools

transmon qubit · multimode 3D flute cavity (TE101 and TE102 modes) · double-sideband microwave driving · characteristic function measurement

Abstract

Two-dimensional massive Dirac systems feature a gapped Dirac-cone dispersion central to a broad range of phenomena in condensed-matter and topological physics. While quantum simulations have demonstrated one-dimensional Dirac dynamics and two-dimensional massless Weyl dynamics, programmable simulation of massive two-dimensional Dirac dynamics remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we realize a programmable two-dimensional free Dirac Hamiltonian in circuit QED, with independently tunable spin-momentum couplings and mass, using a single Rabi-driven qubit coupled to two modes of a multimode cavity. Using this Hamiltonian, we observe rotational Zitterbewegung of a two-dimensional massive Dirac particle and its dependence on the effective mass. Time-dependent master-equation simulations incorporating measured decoherence, corrections beyond the rotating-wave approximation (RWA), and anharmonicity of the transmon reproduce the observed dynamics. Our results establish multimode circuit QED as a compact, programmable platform for higher-dimensional relativistic quantum dynamics and provide a foundation for exploring dynamical and topological phenomena in gapped Dirac systems.

item.title: Probing proximity-induced superconductivity in bilayer graphene using gate-defined quantum dots
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Proximity-induced superconducting gap reaches up to 80 μeV in bilayer graphene contacted by NbSe2 and follows a dwell-time-limited ballistic decay Δ∗(x)=πℏv/(4x) with v≈5.2×104m/s, remaining detectable over distances exceeding 1 μm.

Grade 0.436 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Philipp Schmidt, Mathies Funke, Till Tenger, Katarina Stanojević, Hubert Dulisch, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Fabian Hassler, Christian Volk, Szabolcs Csonka, Christoph Stampfer

Figure

Measured proximity-induced gap Δ∗ as a function of distance x from the NbSe2 edge, showing ballistic 1/x decay across quantum dots defined at four gate locations.

Asks

How does the proximity-induced superconducting gap decay spatially in a gate-defined bilayer graphene channel coupled to a layered superconductor?

But

Base temperature ≈80mK; out-of-plane critical magnetic field Bc≈8mT; effective velocity v extracted near the flattened band edge with order-unity uncertainty.

Tools

bilayer graphene encapsulated in hexagonal boron nitride · few-layer superconducting NbSe₂ · electrostatic split- and finger-gate quantum dot definition · Coulomb blockade and finite-bias tunneling spectroscopy

Abstract

Van der Waals heterostructures offer a direct way of combining two-dimensional (2D) materials with different electronic properties, such as 2D semiconductors, metals, and superconductors, in a single device. Bilayer graphene (BLG) is particularly attractive in this context, as its electrically tunable band gap enables local control of tunnel barriers and quantum dots. Here, we realize an all-2D hybrid platform based on BLG proximitized by superconducting NbSe₂. Using local electrostatic gates, we define tunnel barriers and quantum dots at different distances from the lateral superconductor-semiconductor interface. The quantum dots serve as local spectroscopic probes of the proximitized BLG channel segment, forming tunable superconductor-quantum dot-normal conductor junction devices. Coulomb blockade and finite-bias spectroscopy reveal a proximity-induced superconducting gap of up to 80 μeV and allow to track its evolution with increasing distance from the NbSe₂ contact. We find that the local density of states remains suppressed over distances exceeding 1 μm, consistent with superconducting proximity through a highly ballistic BLG channel. Our results show that BLG-superconductor hybrids offer a controllable platform where quantum dots and quantum point contacts can be well combined with superconductivity.

item.title: Pump-Free Microwave-Optical Bell Pair Generation for Teleportation-Based Quantum Transduction
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Protocol generates microwave-optical heralded Bell pairs without an optical pump, reaching heralding rates up to 3.71 kHz with 0.97 fidelity in a 87Rb ensemble.

Grade 0.428 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…” · Fangxin Li, Jaesung Heo, Zhaoyou Wang, Benjamin Pingault, Xingyu Gao, Tengyang Ruan, Anjun Chu, David D. Awschalom, Andrew N. Cleland, Andrew P. Higginbotham, Alexander A. High, Liang Jiang

Figure

Heralding rate and Bell-state fidelity plotted against transmon relaxation time T1,t across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated platforms.

Asks

Can microwave-optical Bell pairs be generated for teleportation-based transduction without relying on an optical pump?

But

Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes zero optical pump during generation, trapping fields switched off in ensembles, and transmon relaxation time T1,t=300 µs.

Tools

MO-NODE protocol · cavity QED · three-level transmon · Purcell-enhanced emission · single spins, atomic ensembles, and spin-phonon systems

Abstract

The coherent conversion between microwave and optical photons, known as quantum transduction, is critical for connecting superconducting processors to optical networks. Existing methods are limited by complications associated with optical pumping. We propose a pump-free microwave-optical Bell-pair source for teleportation-based transduction. Using a spin or atomic system resonantly coupled to optical and microwave cavities, the scheme generates loss-robust heralded Bell pairs. Across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated systems, this assembly achieves kilohertz-range heralding rates with high fidelity.
